segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I urge you, brothers and sisters, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God; this is your rational worship.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may discern what the will of God is—what is good and pleasing and perfect.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For by the grace given to me I say to every one of you: do not think more highly of yourself than you ought to think, but think with sound thinking, each according to the measure of faith that God has apportioned.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For just as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so we, the many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We have gifts that differ according to the grace given to us: if prophecy, in proportion to our faith;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: if service, in serving; or the one who teaches, in teaching;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: or the one who encourages, in encouraging; the one who shares, with sincerity; the one who leads, with diligence; the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let love be without pretense. Abhor what is evil; cling to what is good.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In brotherly love be devoted to one another; in honor lead the way for one another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In diligence do not be slack; in spirit be fervent; serve the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In hope rejoice; in affliction endure; in prayer persevere.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Share in the needs of the holy ones; pursue hospitality.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Bless those who persecute—bless, and do not curse.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Think of one another in the same way; do not think lofty thoughts, but keep company with the lowly. Do not be wise in your own eyes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Repay no one evil for evil; take thought for what is honorable in the sight of all people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for the wrath, for it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Rather,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for in doing this you will heap burning coals on his head.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good.

notes.note: The Greek adjective was a common word, especially among philosophers, for what belongs to reason or befits a rational being. Many modern versions have “spiritual worship,” taking the contrast to be with animal sacrifice, and the King James Version has “reasonable service.” “Rational” keeps the ordinary sense of the word and fits the stress on the renewed mind in the next verse. The noun translated “worship” is the term for service offered to God in a temple.

The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era. Paul shares the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come. Many versions keep “world” here, but lexicons give “age” as the sense, and some modern translations use it.

notes.traditional: according to the proportion of faith
notes.note: The Greek is literally “according to the proportion of the faith.” Most interpreters take this as the prophet’s own faith, as rendered here. Others take it as “in agreement with the faith,” meaning the content of what is believed. The sentence in verses 6–8 has no main verb in Greek, and many translations supply one such as “let us use them.”

This was an everyday word for serving or carrying out a task for someone, from waiting at table to delivering a commission. It did not name a religious office. Most translations use “ministry” for church work, which now suggests clergy; standard lexicons list “service” among the glosses.

The word’s established sense is singleness or sincerity: giving without mixed motives. Many modern translations render it “generously” or “with generosity,” a sense that fits the context of giving but that lexicographers dispute for this period. The King James Version has “with simplicity.”

notes.traditional: he that ruleth; the one who leads
notes.note: The verb can mean to preside or lead, and also to care for or give aid, as a patron would. Because it stands between sharing and showing mercy, some scholars prefer “the one who gives aid.” Most translations take it as leadership, as here.
The verb literally means to boil. The Greek can refer to the human spirit, as rendered here, or to the Holy Spirit: “be aglow with the Spirit.” Translators and commentators are divided.

The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

Many manuscripts add “you,” and most translations include it. The Greek text followed here omits it. The verb is the same one translated “pursue” in verse 13, so Paul moves from pursuing hospitality to blessing those who pursue with hostile intent.

notes.traditional: men of low estate; the lowly
notes.note: The Greek form can be masculine, meaning lowly people, or neuter, meaning humble tasks or circumstances. The second reading would give “give yourselves to humble things,” in contrast to the “lofty thoughts” just mentioned. Most translations take it of people.

The Greek says only “the wrath,” but the quotation that follows, from Deuteronomy 32:35, shows that God’s judgment is meant. Many translations add “of God” for clarity. The words “says the Lord” are not part of the Deuteronomy text; Paul adds them to mark God as the speaker.

The verse quotes Proverbs 25:21–22 in its Greek form. The meaning of the image is disputed. Most interpreters think it pictures the burning shame an enemy feels when repaid with kindness, which may lead to a change of heart. Others take it as a picture of the divine judgment the enemy will face if unmoved.

The Greek verb is the ordinary word for winning a battle or contest and is related to the noun for “victory.” Most translations have “overcome” here, which in modern English can suggest merely getting past a difficulty. The meaning is not in dispute; “conquer” keeps the note of victory.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations occurs throughout the letters, and translators split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters.”
The verb ranges over urge, appeal, exhort, encourage and comfort, and recurs constantly in Paul and Acts; the senses need fixed renderings.
With its verb λατρεύω it denotes cultic service to God and is rendered variously as “worship” or “service,” which overlaps with the renderings of προσκυνέω and διακονία.
It recurs in Romans and 1 Corinthians as “gift,” “spiritual gift” or “gift of grace,” and its link with χάρις is lost or kept depending on the choice.
It recurs in 2 Corinthians 8–9, Ephesians and Colossians, where versions alternate between “sincerity,” “simplicity” and the lexically disputed “generosity.”
